subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Read: Water Tanks Across India

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens by asking students what they know about where water in their homes comes from. This brief elicitation builds a shared starting point before reading begins.
Teacher reads the informational text aloud (Textbook pp.65–68), pausing to point out the Oorani, Panam Keni, and Tanka as each appears. Students follow along in their books.

Teacher continues the read-aloud through the Punjab water tank section (Textbook pp.68–73), emphasising the sculptural shapes — flowers, roosters, tractors, aeroplanes. Students are encouraged to look at any accompanying illustrations.
Teacher invites two or three students to name one water storage structure they remember from the reading and one tank shape that surprised them. No written response is required at this stage.

periods.teacher_notes: This first encounter with the text lays the factual ground — traditional structures (Oorani, Panam Keni, Tanka) and the sculpted overhead tanks of rural Punjab — that all later work depends on. Read at a measured pace so students absorb the regional vocabulary without pressure. Keep the closing oral exchange quick and inclusive; accuracy is not the point here.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.68): answer four questions on water tanks and Punjab tank designs.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a shared re-reading of the Punjab tank paragraphs (Textbook pp.68–73), asking students to read one sentence each round the class. This re-encounter refreshes the details needed for discussion.

Let us Think — A. (p.68): Teacher poses the first two questions aloud — what we use a water tank for, and where Punjab is located. Students respond orally in pairs before one pair shares with the class; teacher confirms and elaborates.

Let us Think — A. (p.68): Teacher poses questions three and four — how Punjab tanks are made and how their shapes reflect owners' identities. Students discuss in pairs, then the class pools ideas in a brief whole-group share.
Students write answers to all four questions in their notebooks individually. Teacher circulates and gives brief verbal feedback on sentence construction.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the full text read aloud, students are now ready to interrogate it. The fourth question — on identity and tank design — often draws the richest answers; prompt hesitant students by revisiting the text's examples of farmers choosing tractor shapes and sports fans choosing footballs. Flag for students who finish early: the section also mentions water conservation across centuries, which connects to the oracy tasks ahead.

periods.activity_title: Speaking About Water Storage and Personal Choices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p.68): discuss other water storage methods and design your own tank.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recalls the range of traditional water structures in the text — Ooranis, Panam Keni, Tankas — to orient the speaking task. Students are not asked to write anything yet.

Let us Think — B., question 1 (p.68): guided conversation — teacher asks the class to name other ways of storing water beyond overhead tanks. Students contribute examples (pots, dams, ponds, wells, rivers) in a whole-class discussion, with the teacher recording key words on the board.

Let us Think — B., question 2 (p.68): each student thinks quietly for two minutes about what shape they would choose for their own water tank and why, then shares with a partner. Four to five students present their ideas to the class; the teacher probes the 'why' to draw out reasoning.

Quick class count: teacher asks students to raise hands for different categories of tank shapes chosen — animals, vehicles, sports objects, other. The teacher notes the most popular category and invites one student to explain its appeal.

periods.teacher_notes: The second question is the more generative — students often need the first to warm up before they speak freely about personal choices. Encourage specificity: 'a football tank' is a start, but 'because I want my neighbours to know I love cricket' is the level of reasoning the task is after. Students who struggle may be invited to point to an image in the textbook as a scaffold.

periods.activity_title: Group Discussion: Water Wastage and Conservation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak — A. (p.73): group discussion on how we waste water and how to stop it.
Let us Speak — B. (p.73): compile three examples of water wastage and solutions, then share with class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the text's celebration of water conservation across centuries, from ancient Ooranis to modern harvesting systems, to frame why reducing waste matters. Students are seated in groups of three.

Let us Speak — A. (p.73): each group of three discusses how water is wasted in daily life and what can be done. Teacher circulates, prompting groups that stall with the textbook's own example (running water while brushing teeth).
Let us Speak — B. (p.73): each group agrees on at least three examples of wastage with a matching solution and notes them down. One member is chosen to present to the class.
Groups share their examples in turn; the teacher tallies on the board so the class can see which wastage habits came up most often. The class votes on the single most important habit to change.

periods.teacher_notes: Students are likely to name common examples — leaving taps running, watering plants in the midday heat — which is fine; encourage at least one less-obvious example per group. The tally at the end gives the discussion a satisfying collective shape and models simple data gathering, which connects to the informational register of the chapter.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (pp.74–75): listen to passage and choose the correct option for five questions.

homework.task_brief: Let us Listen — C. (p.73): say aloud 'What a tank!' vs 'Water tank' and 'I scream' vs 'Ice cream'; note your answers to the yes/no questions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher tells students they will hear a short story about a day when all water supplies stopped. Students are asked to keep their books closed and listen carefully.
Let us Listen (pp.74–75): teacher reads the passage 'A Day without Water' aloud at a clear, measured pace. The passage is read a second time while students listen with pencils down.

Third reading of the passage (pp.74–75): students may now make brief mental notes. Teacher pauses slightly after each key event (Suma at the tap, school with no water, the tanker arriving, Water Conservation Week).
Students open their textbooks to p.75 and answer the five multiple-choice questions independently. Teacher does not prompt answers but may repeat a section of the passage on student request.

Whole-class verification: teacher reads each question aloud and students call out answers; the teacher confirms the correct option and briefly explains any that caused disagreement, referring back to the passage text.

periods.teacher_notes: Three readings mirror the NCF preparatory guidance for listening tasks. Students who write during the third read are self-scaffolding — allow it. The homework oral task on sound-alike phrases ('What a tank!' / 'Water tank') is brief enough for independent exploration and feeds into the phonics awareness thread of the chapter.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.69): write contractions for six 'not' word pairs.
Let us Learn — B. (p.69): rewrite two paragraphs replacing underlined words with contractions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'are not' and 'aren't' on the board and explains that contractions combine two words, with an apostrophe replacing the missing letters. Two more examples from the chapter text are shown: 'would not' → 'wouldn't', 'did not' → 'didn't'.

Let us Learn — A. (p.69): students write the contractions for the six 'not' pairs in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and checks apostrophe placement; a common error is placing it between the two root words rather than over the omitted letters.

Let us Learn — B. (p.69): teacher reads paragraph 1 about Partho aloud, students identify underlined words. Students rewrite both paragraphs with the correct contractions; teacher moves round the room giving brief individual corrections.
Teacher calls out an underlined phrase from each paragraph and selects a student to give the contraction form aloud. The class confirms, and teacher writes the correct form on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error at this level is writing 'dont' or 'wouldnt' without the apostrophe — spend extra attention on the apostrophe's exact position. The Partho and Tina paragraphs give a meaningful reading context so students encounter contractions in flowing prose rather than isolated drills, which matches the informational text's own register.

periods.activity_title: Exclamatory Sentences and Animal Family Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — C. (p.70): identify exclamatory sentences and name four emotions expressed.
Let us Learn — E. (p.71): read animal family name sets and predict/discuss meaning patterns.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn — D. (p.70): find five exclamatory sentences from Grade 4 English textbook and record them with their emotions in a table.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn — C. (p.70): teacher writes 'He saw a rooster, a tractor, and a giant football, all made of cement!' on the board and asks what makes it an exclamatory sentence. Students identify the exclamation mark and the strong feeling, then name four emotions as prompted in the textbook.

Teacher introduces homework task D (p.70): students will find five exclamatory sentences from their Grade 4 English textbook and note the emotion each expresses in a table. Instructions are clear so the task can be done independently at home.

Let us Learn — E. (p.71): teacher displays the five animal family sets on the board (lion–lioness–lion cub; tiger–tigress–tiger cub; rooster–hen–chick; bull–cow–calf; stallion–mare–foal). Students read each set aloud and the class discusses the pattern — how female and young forms are named. Students copy the sets into their notebooks.
Quick oral quiz: teacher names an animal (e.g. 'bull') and students call out the female and young forms. This brief closing drill fixes the vocabulary through production.

periods.teacher_notes: Exclamatory sentences appear naturally in the chapter — the title 'What a Tank!' is itself a model, and the text's description of sculpted roosters and tractors carries genuine wonder. Draw students' attention to this before moving to the animal families section. The animal family vocabulary (lioness, tigress, mare, foal) is new for most Grade V students; repeat the sets at least twice during the oral quiz.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — F. (p.72): add to and colour the rural Punjab scene illustration.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by connecting the colouring activity to the chapter's celebration of Punjab's artistic tanks — students are invited to add any element that fits a rural Punjab village scene. Colouring pencils and crayons are distributed.
Let us Learn — F. (p.72): students work on the illustration, adding their own elements and colouring. Teacher circulates, asking individual students to name what they are drawing and why.

Word-building bridge from writing task B ahead (p.76): teacher writes 'water', 'power', 'teacher' on the board and elicits the shared ending '-er'. Students call out more '-er' words; then '-or' words (doctor, actor, motor) and '-at' words (flat, chat, bat) are generated the same way. Students jot ten words for each ending in their notebooks.
Three students share their favourite word from each ending list. Teacher confirms and adds any interesting words to the board column.

periods.teacher_notes: The colouring task is genuinely open-ended — a student who draws a football-shaped tank or a rooster on the roof is responding well to the chapter. The word-ending work that follows is light but purposeful: it prepares students for the writing task where they will formally list these word families, and doing it orally first lowers the writing barrier.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (p.76): design and write an awareness poster on saving and cleaning old water tanks.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models a skeleton poster on the board: a topic line ('Save Our Water Tanks — A Community Awareness Campaign'), one sample slogan, two bullet points on why tanks matter, and a fictional cleaning-drive invitation with a place and time. Students observe and ask questions.

Students plan their poster by quickly jotting a slogan idea, two bullet points, and a place-and-time detail in the margin of their page before drafting. Teacher prompts anyone stuck by asking what shape or structure from the chapter they found most surprising.

Let us Write — A. (p.76): students draft and complete their posters in their textbooks or notebooks. Teacher circulates, giving brief feedback on slogan originality, bullet-point clarity, and whether the invitation details (place and time) are present.
Three to four students read their slogans aloud. The class votes on the most memorable one and the teacher explains briefly what made it effective — short, vivid, action-oriented.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes write very general slogans ('Save water'); nudge them toward specificity about tanks ('Clean tanks, safe water', 'Our tank, our pride'). The invitation element — a place and time — is the part most commonly left blank; circulate early to check it is included. The chapter's celebration of tanks as community landmarks makes this a natural real-world writing frame.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — B. (p.76): write ten words each ending in -er, -or, and -at in notebook.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the oral word-building from the previous work on '-er', '-or', and '-at' endings, writing one example of each on the board as a prompt. Students may use those examples as a launchpad.

Let us Write — B. (p.76): students independently write ten words for each ending — '-er', '-or', and '-at' — in their notebooks, organised under three headings. Teacher circulates silently, scanning for real words and correct spelling.

Class comparison: teacher writes three columns on the board (-er, -or, -at). Students call out their words; the teacher writes unique or unusual contributions — this surfaces the range without penalising repetition.

Students check their own lists against the board columns and correct or add words. Teacher draws attention to any word that appears in two columns by sound but different spelling (e.g. 'doctor' vs 'daughter') as a brief curiosity note.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate '-or' and '-er' because they sound the same in many accents; accept both spellings for the same word family in the oral phase but ensure notebooks show the correct written form. Ten words per ending is achievable comfortably in the time — students who finish early can be challenged to find a word for each ending that begins with an unusual letter.

periods.activity_title: The Thirsty Crow: Role-Play and Enactment

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore — B. (p.78): enact the Thirsty Crow story as an interview-style school event.

homework.task_brief: Let us Explore — A. (p.77): find out techniques for cleaning water tanks; note findings and bring relevant pictures for a class chart.

time_bands.activity: Teacher walks students through the four sequential pictures of The Thirsty Crow (Textbook p.78), eliciting what each image shows and how the crow solves its problem. Key vocabulary — pebble, level, pitcher — is confirmed.

Teacher and class plan the enactment together: one student plays the crow, two or three play student interviewers, and others form the audience. Roles are assigned quickly; each interviewer prepares one question to ask the crow about its innovative idea.

Let us Explore — B. (p.78): the enactment runs. The crow answers questions in character, explaining why it chose pebbles, how it knew the water would rise, and what message it has for the school about using clever thinking to solve water problems. Teacher supports with prompts if the crow falters.

Brief class discussion: what does the crow's solution have in common with traditional water structures like the Tanka or Oorani? Students make one connection each, linking the beyond-text activity back to the informational chapter.

Teacher introduces homework task A (p.77): students will find out techniques for cleaning water tanks at home or online, note their findings, and bring any relevant pictures for a class chart to be assembled during a free period. Instructions are given clearly so the task is self-sufficient.

periods.teacher_notes: The Thirsty Crow enactment works best when the crow has a moment to pause and think before answering each interview question — coach the student playing the crow to do this rather than rushing. The closing discussion connecting pebble-raising to ancient water conservation is the most intellectually satisfying move in this unit; allow it to breathe even if the enactment runs slightly long.

items.item_stem: Which of the following water storage structures is found underground in the Thar region of Rajasthan?

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students choosing this may recall Kerala's Panam Keni but confuse its location with Rajasthan.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Students choosing this may confuse Tamil Nadu's Oorani with the Thar region's underground structure.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Students choosing this may know overhead tanks in general but have not linked the Tanka specifically to Rajasthan.

items.item_stem: In the chapter, the sculpted water tanks of rural Punjab are described as reflecting the identity of their owners. In two or three sentences, explain how a tank's shape can show who the owner is, using one example from the text.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The tank's shape shows the owner's interests or job — for example, a farmer might choose a tractor shape because farming is central to their life, while a sports fan might choose a football shape. The text explains that these designs are cultural expressions and tell neighbours something about who lives in the house.

items.item_stem:
Listen as your teacher reads the passage. Then choose the correct answer.

Why did Suma's school close its toilets on the day there was no water?

options.label: B
options.text: Water was not available to use them.

options.label: C
options.text: The school decided to save electricity.

options.label: D
options.text: Students were told to go home early.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students choosing this may infer a common school scenario rather than listening for the water-shortage reason.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Students choosing this confuse water scarcity with a different type of resource saving.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Students choosing this may have missed the detail that school continued but with restrictions.

items.item_stem: Think about the ways water is wasted in daily life that your class discussed, and what the chapter says about traditional water conservation. Speak for about one minute: describe one way you personally waste water and one step you will take to stop it.

expected_elements: Names a specific personal water-wasting habit.
States a clear, realistic step to reduce it.
Speaks in complete sentences for about one minute.

items.item_stem: Write one catchy slogan for a poster about keeping water tanks clean. The slogan should be short, clear, and encourage people to act.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: A good slogan is short (no more than eight words), uses a direct command or a vivid image, and connects cleaning tanks to safe water — for example, 'Clean tanks, safe water for all!' or 'A clean tank is a healthy home.'

expected_elements: Topic heading and original slogan present.
Two bullet points state clear reasons tanks matter.
Cleaning drive invitation includes place and time.

items.item_stem:
Fill in each blank with the correct contraction for the words given in brackets.

1. Suma ________ (could not) believe there was no water.
2. The tanks in rural Punjab ________ (are not) plain at all — they are shaped like flowers and footballs!
3. She ________ (did not) waste water after that experience.
